answers.explanation: Read right to left: the final dot is the root, `edu` is the TLD, `marshall` is second-level, `cs` is a subdomain.
Every lookup can start at the root, which knows the servers for every TLD.
There are 13 root server identities (a through m), and each is copied to many sites around the world using anycast, a trick later in this chapter.
An FQDN has no missing pieces: it names the full path from the host to the root.
Two-letter TLDs belong to countries: `uk`, `de`, `jp`, `ca`. The others are generic TLDs.
They store only delegations: NS records that point to each domain's own nameservers. The domain's servers hold its addresses.
An NS (nameserver) record says "for this zone, ask these servers". Delegation is what lets millions of owners share one tree.
Without a trailing dot, the name is relative, so the server adds the zone's name. Forgetting a dot on a full name gives you mistakes like `mail.example.com.example.com.`
`in-addr.arpa` is still where reverse lookups live today.
